alford-gainesville-1882-02-12.A1:
Beastly "Majah" Alford.
Beastly "Majah" Alford.

Our readers all remember a colored barber and teacher of music who once flourished in Waco, who dubbed himself "Majah Alford, de only fuss-class musician in Waco, sah." "Majah," since giving up ton oral practice and musical pursuits and quitting Waco, has been teaching the young idea how to make night hideous by beating bass-drums and blowing villainous horns, in different parts of the state. It has already been announced to the public that Alford attempted to rape a fourteen-year-old girl of his class at Gainesville, and is now in custody and likely to remain so. Last Sunday it was fortunate for this beast that the guards at the jail could not be intimidated, or he might have been the principal actor at a necktie picnic. From the Gainesville Hesperian we get the following:

"On Sunday last a crowd numbering perhaps fifty or more went to the jail with the avowed intention of taking possession of the "Majah's" precious caress. Happily their demonstrations were confined to talk and theats, and a stand-off from the guards was taken quite submissively. We hope that the good, solid sense of the would-be avengers will show them that there are laws specially applicable to the case now at issue, and when the negro is given a fair trial, his crime, it any, will be speedily punished. To allow "lynch law" to have full scope in a city of our retensions would be a lasting disgrace and work incalculable injury to its prospects, although the crime committed is one of the most heinous known to man."

Alford has been teaching band music and dancing, and will no doubt if the charges against him be proven, do some dancing himself. He has always been a singular character, who feigned to know much more than he really did, and was far too forward with those he could in no wise approach in rank or station. Some years ago he made himself notorious among his race by constituting himself a democratic champion and challenging Gov. Davis to a joint controversy. "Majah" got too sharp to need any more sense or instruction, but had it to give grants to everyone else, and now in his old age he is about to learn a severe lesson.

c-d-owens-tampa-1882-03-06.A1:
Lynching in Tampa.
Special dispatch to Jacksonville Times.]
TAMPA FLORIDA March 6
A tramp (man) named Charles Owens, was hanged in a street of Tampa, between two and three o'clock P. M. to-day, by an outraged community for burglariously entering a house near town last night and assaulting, with intent to commit rape upon, one of our most respectable young ladies. He made a confession of his guilt before meeting his fate. JOHN P. WALL.

A correspondent of the Times, under date of March 7th, gives the following graphic account of the whole affair:

Yesterday at half-past two o'clock there occurred here one of the most awful tragedies that I ever witnessed, and the like of which has not occurred in the United States in the past twenty-four years. A prisoner, without trial, was taken from the jail, while the U. S. District Court was in session not ten steps away, carried across the street in front of the court-house and hanged to a shade tree. This occurred in open daylight, right in the centre of a town of over a thousand population.

THE CRIME.

The victim was a young white man about thirty years old, and of medium size and height, named C. D. Owens. His resemblance to Guiteau was remarkable. He came to this country from London about a year ago, and has been working at different little jobs, and making but a poor livelihood. On last Sunday afternoon he was seen in town rather the worse for liquor. Sunday night a person broke into the residence of one of our prominent citizens on Nebraska Avenue, and after committing several small thefts entered the sleeping apartment of a highly respectable young l
cape, leaving his victim in a fainting and almost dying condition. The neighbors were at once summoned and a search was promptly begun. THE PURSUIT. For fear of exciting the community, the matter was kept a profound secret and only the officers of the law and a few immediate friends knew anything about the case until the scoundrel was locked safely in jail. The sheriff and a posse
c-d-owens-tampa-1882-03-06.A2:
started in pursuit at about ten o'clock yesterday. They got a clew and followed it up and at twelve o'clock they overtook Owens beyond Krause's Spring, and after slight resistance captured him. Owens acknowledged to being in the house Sunday night, but said he only intended robbery. Afterwards he said he thought of rape, and then said he ought to have murdered the girl and hushed the matter up.

THE INFURIATED MOB.

He appeared to take the entire matter as a huge joke from the time he was arrested. In coming back to town, as he crossed the river, he threw a package overboard. He was placed in jail at about one o'clock. In the meantime the news of the intended rape had got wind and spread, and by the time the prisoner was safely behind the bars, the people had about determined to take the law in their own hands. In an hour's time an immense crowd had gathered, and a vote was called, and all who favored taking Owens out and hanging him to a tree were asked to step out. Nearly all stepped out. Then about twenty men volunteered to go up to the sheriff's home and get the jail keys. I am sure Mr. Craft did not think for a moment that the crowd intended harm. When the mob entered the sheriff's house, he was at his dinner. As he rose from the table a dozen pair of hands grabbed him, and before he knew what he was about, his keys were gone and the mob with them. The infuriated mob pressed on towards the jail. In the meantime the mob was growing larger every moment. The jail door was unlocked, and the prisoner was taken out. He was the most unconcerned and indifferent person present. He said: "Oh, you all can't bull-doze me. I will have a trial." Then he was hurried across the court-house yard, and then across the street under a large shade tree. A rope was passed over a limb, a noose made, and his hands were tied. Now, for the first time, the miserable wretch realized his fate. Before, he did not know what to think. I am sure he had no idea of being hung. As soon as he saw that the mob was in earnest, then he denied the crime and begged for his life. He said he would go to prison for life if only mercy were shown him. He begged for a trial, and the grimmest reply was given I ever heard: "Yes, we will give you a trial, but we will hang you first and try you afterwards."

THE LYNCHING.

Lieutenant Danes, of the Third Artillery, arrived on the ground, and as soon as he saw how matters stood he called the garrison to arms to rescue the prisoner. The sheriff had come down and the mayor of the town, and they were now all begging for the prisoner's life. The poor, friendless wretch saw that if he could only prolong his life a few minutes the troops in the garrison would rescue him. How he fought, how he begged for time, how he called on the crowd to help him! But in vain. The fair face of his intended victim was uppermost in the minds of the maddened throng. As soon as the teet and hands of the doomed man were tied a dray was driven under the tree and Owens placed thereon. When the dray moved off the rope slipped and the prisoner fell to the ground. The military were expected every moment, and now the mob must act quickly. So a half a dozen ready hands laid hold of the rope and drew the body of C. D. Owens up.

There the body hung in the public streets, out in front of the hall of justice, court sitting from day to day; there the body hung till sunset. The crowd slowly dispersed, the military did not come, and human vengeance was visited swiftly on this wretched man. May the God he has gone to meet have more mercy on him than did his fellowmen!

c-d-owens-tampa-1882-03-06.A4:
Murderer Lynched.
The March 4th.
PENSECOLA, Fla., March 18.—At Tampa today a young Englishman named C. D. Owens attacked a young lady with a knife and stabbed her nearly to death. He was captured and placed in jail, but within an hour he was taken out by a mob and hanged to a shade tree in the court house, where the United States court was in session at the time. The mayor and sheriff protested, and Lieut Danes, of the Third United States artillery, ordered out the troops to rescue the prisoner, but before the troops arrived Owens was a dead man.

The second call came off somewhat easier, prices at 9 to 10 points higher than yesterday. Those yesterday were short, covered early in the day and others purchased, because they think expedient to avail of every decline, considering there can be but little short. Wm. Miles, of Giles county, Tenn., married his step-daughter recently.

A Stalwart in Jacksonville, Fla., has named his last male heir Arthur Ulysses Roscoe.

The Tuscumb'a Democrat has heard of some negroes in the destitute section of North Alabama who sustain life by eating parched cotton seed.

Gen. Bradlock, the hero of the historic defeat, has four grandchildren in Jefferson county Fla., whose aggregate ages sum up 407 years.

Several bales of cotton were brought to Augusta last week from the estate of a recently deceased planter, which had been raised before the war. Some of it was in good condition, but the bagging had decayed and dropped from the bales.

Last week a man named C. D. Owens was hung by a mob in Tampa, Florida, just across the street from the jail, in broad daylight, while the United States district court was in session. He had attempted to commit a rape, and failing, had tried to kill his victim.

Four men went to the house of M. J. Fowler, near Blue Point, Alabama, disguised, and, while one guarded his wife, the other three gave him a terrible beating, thirty-six lashes being counted on his back the next day. The only offense he had committed was running off with a young lady and marrying her.

A native Tennessee arrived in Chattanooga on Monday from Washington territory. He had become dissatisfied out there, and not having the money to return by rail, had bought a mule and ridden 650 miles, then took a skiff and rowed down the Yellowstone 1,250 miles to Bismark, where he got on the train and came the rest of the way.

A lady in Raleigh, North Carolina, lost a gold watch, socket and chain on June 20, 1860, supposing it at the time to have been stolen. A few days ago a servant, in raking under the barn for eggs, pulled out the missing articles in almost as good condition as when last seen, the morocco case containing them, though, having been rotted away on the side next the ground.

Tampa Tribune, March 16.]
Tampa Tribune, March 16.]
Judge Locke vs. General Wall.
The action of any official is a legitimate rule.
Judge Locke vs. General Wall.

The action of any official is a legitimate subject of criticism, and probably none is more deserving of a critical review than that of a Judge when arbitrarily exercising the rights and powers with which he is invested as a court. On the second day of the Spring Term of the United States Court here last week, Judge Locke issued a rule against General J. B. Wall to show cause why he should not be stricken from the roll of attorneys practicing in his court for counselling and aiding in the unlawful hanging of a man in Tampa, on the 6th inst. General Wall very properly refused to put in an answer to such an accusation, but respectfully asked the court to waive the rule until after the Spring Term of the State court in this county, which would be holden this month. This Judge Locke refused to do, and last Friday issued an order disbarring General Wall until further order of the court.

In this act Judge Locke proceeded in a manner wholly at variance with the rulings of the Supreme Courts of the United States and of Florida, as was plainly demonstrated by Colonel Sparkman last Saturday in an argument before his court on a motion to vacate the order disbarring Mr. Wall, in not basing his rule on a sworn complaint, which both these courts have enunciated as necessary and requisite before the issue of the rule to show cause, &c. Instead of waiting for any such sworn complaint, Judge Locke issued the rule on hearsay, and a day or two subsequently called on the United States Marshal of his court to testify against General Wall; but even his evidence did not substantiate the facts alleged in the rule calling on General Wall to show cause, &c. This is a fair statement of the case and the law points involved, but we reserve our comments for another issue.
c-d-owens-tampa-1882-03-06.A23:
Florida Affairs.
The French steamship Orpal struck on a shoal reef near Key West the past week, but was relieved by Capt. She Dave's boat, who received $5,000 for the job. The money was in kegs, and before Dave's boat reached land a squall struck it and the money kegs rolled overboard.

Gen. J. B. Wall, of Tampa, has applied to the Supreme Court of the United States for a mandamus to compel Judge Locke to vacate his order temporarily suspending him from practicing in the United States Court for participating in the lynching of Owens.

Jacksonville Union: "A few days since Mr. Wm. Cox, living near the eleven mile post, on the old King's road, was shot in the arm by O. P. Johnson. It seems that the two men were friends, and while Cox was engaged in work Johnson came up, and leveling his gun on Cox, told him to up his hands. Cox at once threw up his hands, and Johnson, not knowing that the gun was loaded, pulled the trigger with the above effect. Cox was brought to the city, his arm was dressed by Dr. Fernandez, and he is now getting along as well as could be expected."

Tallahassee Floridian: "Last week there appeared in the Floridian an item stating that the ladies of the Philadelphia Silk Culture Association were preparing a silk gown to be presented to Mrs. Garfield, and claiming for it the distinction of being the first entirely American made silk fabric. During the past week we have been informed by a lady that many years ago Mrs. Blocker, the former wife of Capt. H. T. Blocker, hatched the egg, raised the worms, reeled and spun the silk, wove it, and cut and made herself a dress, which ante-dates the Philadelphia garment by many years."

Correspondence Florida Union: "The first shovel of dirt on the Green Cove Spring and Melrose Railroad was thrown on Tuesday by General Superintendent A. F. Vogelbach, followed by shovels thrown by Hon. C. B. Dungan, President of the Chester Construction Company, and by Hon. R. B. Canova, the veteran worker for the G. C. S. & M. R. R., and by R. W. Davis, Secretary and Attorney for the same. Major N. B. Clinch and many citizens joined in the ceremony, amid the boom of cannon. Active construction has commenced and the work will be pushed through without delay. The present terminus is Melrose, but the road will go through to Gainesville. This will give quicker time from the interior to Jacksonville than by any other road."

Tallahassee Floridian: "Mr L. Raney, live in near Moccasin Gap, in this county, some weeks since employed a colored man to clean out and deepen an old well that had been abandoned many years ago, and had caved in and filled up to within a few feet of the surface. When the man had reached a depth of about twenty-five feet he found a post in the centre of the well—a hewn post about the size and length of an ordinary fence post. He dug deep enough to enable him to remove the post, and when he pulled it out of the earth a stream of water came pouring into the well, and before he could be drawn out the water was three or feet deep all around him. In a few minutes the water suddenly disappeared, he again descended into the well, and found a hole in the centre of it, and could hear water running beneath. He could not reach the water with a ten foot pole, and as he was not anxious to emigrate by the subterranean 'short line,' he abandoned the job."

emma-johnson-summerfield-1882-03-15.A1:
FLASHES FROM MACON.
Big Blaze in Cotton-A Citizen Buried in the Ruins-An Old Man Butchered by a Young Negress.
MACON, March 15 — A fire this morning, supposed to be accidental, broke out in the warehouse of C. D. Anderson & Son, on Fourth street. The flames soon enveloped the building and rapidly spread to the paper and rag warehouse of Wolff & Bro., and continued its work.

R. B. Watson, formerly a prominent cotton broker, is supposed to be buried beneath the debris, and his remains will be taken out to-morrow.

The total loss is $50,000, on which there was $21,500 insurance. Cotton was stored in the warehouse belonging to different parties, and nearly all of it was damaged. The firemen behaved splendidly.

At Summerfield, six miles from here, an old man named William A. Evans was foully murdered last night by Emma Johnson, colored, who used an axe to perpetrate the deed. Evans was in bed, and the blows were struck in the dark. The murderess was arrested and is now confined in jail.

She persistently denies any connection with the crime, but the evidence is conclusive. The murder was committed in Evans' store and for the sake of plunder. Emma is about sixteen years old, and seems perfectly indifferent.

At Summerfield the officers were surrounded by a mob of white and coated people, but by strenuous efforts lynching was prevented.
emma-johnson-summerfield-1882-03-15.A2:
Murdered.
MACON, GA., March 15.—W. R. Evans, a merchant of Summerfield, about six miles from Macon, was murdered in bed last night by a negro woman named Johnson, alias Carrie Wassey, to whom Mr. Evans had given a night's lodging. Her object was robbery, but the groans of the dying man brought assistance. The woman was arrested and brought to Macon this morning. At Summerfield the officers were surrounded by a mob of white and colored people, but by strenuous efforts lynching was prevented.

A DIABOLICAL GEORGIA MURDER.
THE PERPETRATOR BEFRIENDED BY HER VIC-TIM—LYNCH LAW THREATENED.
MACON, GA., March 15.—William A. Evans, a merchant of Summerfield, six miles from Macon, was murdered in bed last night by a negro woman named Emma Johnson alias Carrie Massie, to whom Evans had kindly given a night's lodging. The object was robbery, but the groans of the dying man brought assistance. The woman was brought to Macon this evening. At Summerfield the officers were surrounded by a mob of white and colored people, but by strenuous efforts a lynching was prevented.

Georgia Affairs.

The poles put up by the Fuller Electric Light Company in Augusta have been taken down, and the bright vision has faded.

The Stephens Fire Company, the victors in the contest in Augusta, and later at Charlotte, have been tendered a public dinner by way of compliment to their excellence.

It is said that about seventy reapers have been sold by one firm in Madison this year.

Washington shipped its first crate of peaches of this year's crop on Monday.

The late frosts nipped the young cotton in our northern counties.

The experiment with the electric light at the Muscogee Mills on Monday worked to the satisfaction of all concerned. It is probable that the whole city of Columbus will be lighted up by electricity.

As the Southwestern Railroad passenger train ran on the Flint river bridge Monday afternoon a twelve-year-old tramp was found perched on the trucks under the passenger coach stealing a ride. The train was stopped and the youthful cosmopolitan rescued from his perilous position.

The case of the State vs. Carrie Massey, colored, charged with the murder of William Evans, in Summerfield, Bibb county, a short while ago, was marked for trial yesterday at Macon. The Telegraph and Messenger says that the case will be one of the most interesting of the term, as there is much more in it than has been given to the public.

Only two cases of small-pox developed in Atlanta during Sunday and Monday, although Sunday was very generally regarded by physicians as the last day of the period in which a fresh lot of cases might have reasonably been expected. The two cases were found Sunday and none were reported Monday. Thus it will be seen that the scare is about over, and that no cause for uneasiness any longer exists.

The wheat crop now being harvested in Jasper county is one of the very best ever produced there. There was a large area sown in fall oats, and they are about as good as the land, under any circumstances, could produce. The yield will be immense. Spring oats are not so good, but the recent rain will greatly improve the prospect.

The Butler Herald reports that Messrs. Peed & Halley have quite a curiosity at their store. Mr. J. L. Parker, while out in the woods a few days ago, discovered a fox den, in which were two young gray foxes, scarcely old enough to have their eyes opened. One of these animals Mr. Parker secured and brought to town, the other one having been carried away during his absence by the mother of the brutes. Messrs. Peed & Halley having a cat that had recently lost a brood of young kittens, the fox was given to her, and is now being nursed and raised by the cat with perfect care and devotion.

Three ladies and four gentlemen were baptised at Shallowford, about four miles from Gamesville, on Sunday.

Atlanta Post Appeal: "Two more victims are added to the pernicious influence of dime literature. Yesterday afternoon two little colored boys, Tommy Simonton and Aleck Wade, aged about twelve years, and living at M Vine street, while out for a Sunday stroll with a plum orchard in view, were sighted by a couple of white youths, alleged to be Walter Smith and Frank Wilson, going quietly down the road, who, taking them for bandits, probably Masters Smith and Wilson held a council of war, and Masters Smith, as it is alleged, fired upon the youthful colored pair, lodging a ball in the stomach of Tommy Simonton; firing again, the ball struck the left hand of young Wade. Much excitement was created in the vicinity of the tragedy, and it was not known who was responsible for the deed until the white infants mentioned were brought to the house, where they were recognized by the sufferers as the authors of their indisposition. The boys were arrested and lodged in the station house to await trial this afternoon."

He attempted a vote against the board at the recent Pharmaceutical Convention, and signally failed. After this he applied for a mandamus in the courts restraining the Board of Examiners from charging a druggist's license fee. This decision sustains the board in the effort to elevate the profession by allowing none to compound druggists' prescriptions but regular licensed and competent pharmacists."

Mowre Advertiser: "The other day the people of Forswyth were astonished to see four men march into town, bound and under the command of Mr James Krug. They kept up the line of march until they reached the jail. Their names are Sol Dillard, George Calhoun, Dave Hogan and Andy Taylor, and they are charged with burglary from the house of Mr John L. Ponder, who lives a few miles from Forswyth. For a long time—perhaps a year or more—Mr. Ponder has been missing articles from his house, his barn and smoke house, and he could not account for their disappearance. Finally he went into a long and patient investigation of the matter, and the result was the arrest of the four persons named. There is evidence that this party had been engaged in a system of combined pillage, and that they had keys to fit all the locks about Mr. Ponder's house—including the trunks, etc. A five-dollar bill was taken from Mrs. Ponder's trunk, which was all the time kept locked. Perhaps $20 in money have been stolen from the house, besides other things, the value of which cannot be estimated."

Home Courier: "Mr. Quinn, of the United States Fish Commission, arrived in the city yesterday morning in a special car, bringing with him 1,200 small shad to be deposited in our rivers. Soon after the car arrived, Mr. Wm. Quinn and his assistance hauled seventeen large canns, containing six hundred thousand of the little fish, to the lower wharf—just above the junction of the two river—and emptied them into the Etowah. An equal number were then carried a short distance up the Oostanaula and deposited in that stream. These little fellows were only four days old when launched into the stream, though at that age appeared able to shift for themselves and take their chances with the big seventy five pounds cat fish which infest the rivers. While there is a glut of Georgia peaches in one market there are se res of other markets in which they would bring fancy prices if they could only be had. We shall, therefore, continue to insist on the railroads and carrying companies giving better facilities, and if we can only see as much accomplished next year as has been done this year the problem of transporting fruit will have been nearly solved. In the meantime it is important that the present crop shall be fully utilized. If it cannot be marketed as green fruit, it should be canned or dried. In either of these shapes it will command world-wide markets and good prices. As dried fruit or canned, it can be shipped at the lowest freight rates, and if there is a glut in the market, it can be stored until the glut is over. Last year, a remarkably poor fruit year, over $10,000 of good money went into Griffin alone for dried fruit. That plucky little city should get not less than $100,000 for dried peaches this year. Georgia is less than 400 miles from the centre of population of the country, and it is folly to say that, in one shape or other, we cannot market profitably our fruit crop. California is over 3,000 miles from the centre of population, and yet she realizes more from her fruit crop than she does from her wheat."

On Saturday night last some party or parties fired the corn crib of Mr. J. L. Hall, in Laurens county, and discharged a pistol to attract the attention of the family. The inmates of the house rushed out, and in their absence the dwelling was entered and robbed of a trunk containing money and valuable papers. The trunk was found later broken open. Four negroes have been arresed on suspicion.

One of the machines for the electric light company has arrived at Columbus. The company will begin operations as soon as the full complement of machinery is received.

A company is now being organized at Athens to start a laboratory for the wholesale manufacture of drugists' chemicals of all kinds.

Love Wilder, express messenger between Albany and Smithville, met with quite a serious accident Tuesday. He was dismounting from the express wagon from the rear, when his foot caught in some way, and he was thrown violently against the edge of the depot platform upon his stomach.

J. H. Garner arrested Jack Jones, colored, in Newman last Tuesday, upon the charge of murder, it being supposed that he is the individual who shot Chandler Arnold on the night of the 38th of December, ult., and for whose arrest and conviction the Governor offered a reward of $150.

The Ciceronian and Phi Delta societies of Mercer University have sent a challenge to the Demosthenian and Phi Kappa, of the Georgia University, to meet them in debate, in Macon, on the 38th of June next, during Mercer commencement. The challenge has been accepted, and a few days since the Demosthenian and Phi Kappa societies met and selected their representatives. These are Messrs. P. H. Bell, of Atlanta; H. V. Washington, of Macon; and H. H. Phinizy, of Athens. The Mercer representatives have not yet been selected, nor has the subject of debate been chosen.

Mr. R. T. Bean, a married man, and Mrs. Ariminta Thompson, a married woman, both of Newnan, left their families Tuesday morning and tied the town on an elopement tour. They went to Atlanta together, but soon after their arrival the Sheriff of Coweta county put in an appearance in search of the couple. With the aid of Atlanta officers not much time was wasted in finding the parties, and they were promptly arrested. The man and woman were handcuffed and locked together, and in this condition carried back to Newnan under the surveillance of the Sheriff.

It is thought that two white tramps burned the house of Floyd King, in Oconee, a few nights ago, as they were seen hanging around the neighborhood, and two tracks were found around the building next morning. King is an industrious colored man, who accumulated some $5,000 since the war.

One day last week a little child of Thomas Gunter, who lives on R. B. Mathew's place in Oglethorpe, was missed, and search being instituted, it was soon found in a tub of water with life, to all appearances, extinct. After hard work, however, it was brought to, and has entirely recovered.

Athens Watchman: "A Northern company (supposed to be the Inman) last Saturday closed a trade for the Barnett Snooks property. They paid $22,500 for the Oconee side, including a half mile of fall and 60) acres of land, and $100 for Mrs. Tinsdal's property opposite, with 70 acres. At the July term of Oconee Court a charter will be granted and work will commence at once. They will spend $750,000 preparing the land for manufactories."

Augusta Chronicle, 10th: "Last evening at six o'clock a stiff westerly wind sprang up and blew the dust into the air. From the western sky a black, stringy mass of clouds began to drive across the heavens, and rumbling, funnel shaped clouds, with pent up winds, bygan to whir through the air. For a while the atmosphere was dense and dark, and it looked as if w cyclone had struck the town. Signs were knocked down and limbs of trees were scattered about. The cyclone—for such it was—jumped over Augusta, fortunately for the city, and bounded across the river into Carolina. We have not heard of any damage being done. After the breeze the air was several degrees colder, and a hard shower sprang up, which continued for some time."

Columbus Enquirer-Sun, 9th: "Last night an Enquirer-Sun reporter met Lieutenant Wiley, of the Macon police force, on our street, and feeling assured that something unusual was on the tapis, he put to work his reportorial gimlet. As the result the reporter learned that Lieutenant Wiley had been in this community in search of George Radford, colored, wanted for murder in Crawford county, and that he succeeded in capturing him yesterday about noon on the plantation of Mr. William Byrd, about six miles from this city, in Alabama Radford got into a dispute with a negro named Golden over a game of cards in Crawford county in May, 18:0, and killed him. He fled the county, and has been in the neighborhood of Mr. Byrd's plantation ever since. A reward of one hundred dollars was offered for his capture. Lieutenant Wiley brought his prisoner to this city, and placed him in the guard house until eleven o'clock last night, when he left with him for Macon."

Atlanta Post Appeal, 9th: "The latest scheme for swindling citizens was developed this morning by the operations of two sharpers along Luckie street. A smooth faced young man canvassed the street yesterday morning with packages of needles, which he left for examination and called for in the afternoon in case no sale could be effected. In a large majority of cases the goods were returned. This morning the same young man, accompanied by an accomplice who waited outside, made another tour of the street. He made a peremptory demand for the return of the needles or the payment of twenty-five cents, the price asked. At one house where he called the head of the family happened to be at home, as also a visitor who had witnessed the return of the needles. In spite of the overwhelming evidence, the fellow tried in the most insulting manner to force the family to refund the money he claimed was due. He had the discretion, however, to retire in good order about three feet in advance of the husband's boot."

Augusta Chronicle: "The trial of the case of William H. Johnson vs. the Georgia Railroad, for $10,000, suit for damages, was concluded at Morgan Superior Court on Wednesday. Dr. Godfrey has ordered a few bushels of seed rice from Savannah, and will try four acres in it. Shooting and Killing at Hackberry.
On Monday last a man by the name of Weldon, an employee of the surveying party of the Atlantic and Pacific R. R. Co., went into Hackberry ostensibly for the purpose of killing a man by the name of Bronco Pat, whom he had failed to find, but filled up on benzine and fired a shot at Doctor Day, missing his mark.

Day departed from the scene of troubles and met Johnny Bullock, a stage driver whom he invited to accompany him and have a "smile." Upon entering the saloon, Bullock commenced jesting with Weldon when he shot Bullock three times, killing him. Weldon tried to escape, but was captured by a ball from the six-shooter of Charley Spencer, the Scout. Weldon is seriously shot, and perhaps lynched ere this.
j-o-weldon-mineral-park-1882-02-21.A4:
A MURDERER LYNCHED.
SAN FRANCISCO, Feb. 25.—A dispatch from Mineral Park, Ariz., says: At Hackberry, about thirty miles from this town, J. O. Weldon, a desperate character, on the 20th inst., shot and killed a peaceable citizen named John Bullock, without provocation. The people opened fire on Weldon. He returned it, slightly wounding Indian Agent Charles Spencer. Weldon was shot through the breast, and after his pistol was emptied, surrendered. He was held in custody till the night of the 21st, when a party of fifteen men took him out and hanged him to a beam of a blacksmith shop. Weldon declared publicly a short time ago that he was glad that Guiteau had killed President Garfield.

ARIZONA.
ARIZONA.
A Bad Man Lynched.
PEAL PARK. FEBHURY 921.
A Bad Man Lynched.
MINERAL PARK, February 231 (via Prescott, February 25th).—News has just reached the Alta Arizona office of a dreadful tragedy at Hackley, thirty miles from this town. J. O. Weldon, a desperate character, on the 20th instant, shot and almost instantly killed, without any provocation, a good and peaceable citizen by the name of John Bullock. The citizens immediately rushed to the scene of the shooting and opened fire on Weldon, which he returned, slightly wounding Indian Agent Charles Spencer. The citizens at length shot Weldon through the breast, and, after his pistol was emptied, he surrendered. He was held in custody by Deputy Sheriff Davis till the night of the 21st, when a party of fifteen men took him out and hanged him to the beam of a blacksmith shop. Weldon declared publicly, a short time ago, that he was glad that Guiteau had killed Garfield.

NEWS OF THE DAY.
CRIME AND CRIMINALS.
RECENT DISASTERS AND SENSATIONS.
What Has Been Agitating the Country.

J. H. Hughes, known as the "Fakir of Ava," is dangerously ill in Troy, N. Y., from the bite of a pet raccoon.

Edward Moore, of Trenton, N. J., reported suffering from hydrophobia, died at noon on Saturday.

Four gamblers from Detroit quarreled on a railroad train near Shalford, Ontario, last Friday night, and one of them, named Johnson, was mortally wounded.

A respectable colored man named Hayes, 24 years of age, was shot dead while trying to make peace between several other colored men who were quarreling in Montreal on Saturday.

The president has signed the joint resolution appropriating $100,000 for the relief of the sufferers by the flood in the Mississippi valley.

J. O. Weldon, a murderer and notorious ruffian generally, was taken from the jail on the night of the 21st inst. and lynched by a mob.

At the Webster night school in St. Louis, on Friday night, Wilhelm Manenthal, 12 years of age, stabbed another pupil named Fuchs, who had been mocking and maltreating him. It is feared Fuchs will not recover.

Two men, named Moutray and Massip, quarreled about some property in Blanchard, Ontario, on Saturday, when Moutray shot Massip in the breast and then shot himself. Both are fatally wounded.

The bodies of the family buried under a snowslide in Big Cottonwood canyon, near Salt Lake City, have been recovered. All were found lying in their beds, and it was evident they had been smothered in their sleep.

John Knoppel, aged 30 years, a confectioner, living at 1,221 Olive street, Philadelphia, committed suicide by stabbing himself in the heart with a pair of scissors.

D. J. Murphy, ex-district attorney, was shot and perhaps fatally wounded by John Moroney, a policeman, in the police court, at San Francisco, on Saturday morning. Moroney, who had been a witness in a case against a client of Murphy, was referred to by the latter as an Australian convict and thief.

The prisoners in the jail at Lagrange, Texas, attempted to escape on Friday night. One of them got off, but another, named Harrison, was shot dead by the sheriff.

William Beecher, 23 years of age, quarreled with another man at Etaa, near Allegheny City, Penna., on Saturday night and was stabbed to death by a drunken man named Wolff, who came up and became greatly exasperated because the others paid no attention to him. Wolff is in jail.

Samuel Hill, a quack doctor, was found murdered in his night clothes in a ditch near his house in Southampton county, Virginia, last Friday night. The house was burned. It is supposed Hill was killed by some colored men in revenge for the death of a patient for whom he had prescribed, and whom he was suspected of poisoning.

A young man, named Deering, accused of horse stealing, was taken from an officer and lynched near Gatesville, Texas, a few days ago. On Saturday a hundred armed neighbors of Deering rode into the town and demanded the arrest of the lynchers "or they would take the law into their own hands." The sheriff, under this threat, arrested a man named Leavitt and his two sons, and at last accounts was searching for others of the lynchers.

Losses by Fire.

Mrs. Benjamin Finch was burned to death in Prince George county, Virginia, on Friday night by her dress becoming ignited from an open fire at which she was sitting.

The grocery store of Solomon Brothers, in Savannah, Georgia, was destroyed by the last night. The store is at
the grocery store of Solomon Brothers, in Savannah, Georgia, was destroyed by fire last night. The loss is stated at $90,000.

The steamboat Bertie Claiborne has been burned to the water's edge at Steel's Bayou, Mississippi. The loss on the boat and cargo is $15,000. A colored man and three children were drowned.

The boot shop of S. Fullam & Co., at West Brookfield, Massachusetts, was destroyed on Saturday morning by an incendiary fire. Loss, $40,000. A fireman was seriously injured by a falling brick.

Putnam & Brooks' confectionery at Grand Rapids, Michigan, was burned. Loss, $40,000.

The loss by the fire last Friday night in the building occupied by Aiken, Insey & Co., in Baltimore, is estimated at $27,000.

Flood, Explosion and Wreck.

The levee at Shawneetown, Illinois, broke on Friday, and the town was flooded.

Michael Stulzman, the remaining victim of the boiler explosion at Carlisle, Ohio, died on Saturday, making in all six deaths.

The brigantine John Laughlin, of Philadelphia, from Pensacola for Aspinwall, with lumber, was wrecked on January 29th, north of Old Providence Island. She is a total loss, but part of her cargo may be saved. Her crew have arrived at Aspinwall.

The levee at Friar's Point, Mississippi, was in danger. The cattle at that place were "wading about with only their heads above water," and in many of the houses not yet swept away the people are forced to sleep on the roofs. Few houses were habitable on the first floor.

An explosion occurred on Saturday afternoon at the foundry of S. B. Sargent & Co., New Haven, by which five men were injured, two seriously. with the cupola, which contained several tons of melted iron and coal, and when the bottom was opened the fiery mass dropped into the water, creating superheated steam. The damage to the building was slight.

A five-story brick building in St. Louis, occupied by Kroft, Holmes & Co., wholesale grocers, tumbled down with a crash at half past two o'clock on Saturday morning, and became a heap of ruins. The loss on building and stock is probably over $50,000. The building, which seems
j-o-weldon-mineral-park-1882-02-21.A17:
MONDAY.
Enjoyable places—Theatres and heaven.
Whitney & Ellis are having a big run of custom. They are gentlemen deserving of success.
Snow, the beautiful snow, made us another visit.
The estate of the late Cornelius Ramas has been s ttled up by Judge Brooks, the Administrator.
Prescott should have a Board of Trade. Organize, gentlemen.
Capt. Atchison, of Mineral Park, goes home to-morrow, Tuesday, per stage.
Several very important mining sales are on the eve of being made in this county.
The Signal mill is working away successfully. The bullion output is large from that direction.
One of John R. Price & Co's teams arrived to-day from the R. R. for a load of powder, etc.
To-day has been pleasant and the roads commenced drying up, much to the satisfaction of all.
Mohave county, with her fine mining properties, must attract attention from the outside world.
The Tiptop mine, at a depth of between six and seven hundred feet, is richer than ever. What will it be at a depth of 2,000 feet?
Work on the Black Warrior has been resumed, and soon we may hear of rich strikes, big sale or the working of ere in that direction.
W. W. Cook and J. D. Cook arrived last evening from New River, where they have a large dairy.
February has but 22 days, consequently Wednesday next, the 29th, will be the 1st day of March.
Mr. Dewey, of Chicago, and Mr. Blandy, of Turkey Creek, came in to-day from the Black Hills mining district.

Mr. Rehm offers his one-half interest in the Prescott Keg Saloon and Lodging House for sale, which will be seen in this issue of the MINER.

D. C. Thorne will start up his chop house in a day or two in bon ton style. Everything is to be in apple pie order and of metropolitan array.

The Alta says that the ElDorado mine, in Gold Basin, is about to change hands. Some gentlemen from Silver Reef are negotiating its purchase.

Henry Ward Beecher is to visit Arizona this Spring. We hear that he comes to Northern Arizona and will go to the Grand Canyon of the Colorado.

Sargent, of California, has been nominated by the President for Secretary of the Interior. There will be a fight in the Senate over his confirmation.

Doctor Taggart, of Yuma, who was shot by a worthless fellow, is said to be in great danger of losing his life. The Doctor killed the man who attacked him.

The Navajoe Indians are the richest tribe in the West. They have fine herds of horses, cattle and sheep. Their lands embrace some of the most valuable coal fields in America.

There will be a meeting of Aztlan Lodge No. 177, F. & A. M., this evening at 7:45 o'clock for work in the third degree. All Master Masons in good standing are cordially invited.

Is it possible that we are to have another drug store in Prescott. People on the outside who fail to find the drug business advertised are under the impression that we are without these necessary luxuries.

The Dosoris people are running a tunnel in on the mine 500 feet, which will tap the ledge 350 feet beneath the surface. That will test fairly the value of the now very promising Dosoris mine.

Weldon, who murdered John Bullock at Mineral Park last week, was lynched by the law abiding citizens of that place on the eve ning of the sad affair. Another brave has been sent to his Maker without judge or jury interfering.

Sam Purdy, Jr., has gone to San Francisco for the purpose of attending to the business of his father, who died in that city last week quite suddenly. Samuel Purdy, Sr., was a man honorable in his dealings and much respected by all.

We hear of a gent who is coming to our city for the purpose of manufacturing cigars. He proposes to manufacture from the finest tobacco and sell at living prices. We invite him to come and advertise his business in the MINER.

Geo. Tyng, who has been on the Isthmus superintending the construction of the Tehauntepec Canal for three years, at a salary of $9,000 per annum, has so far lost his health that he has decided to return to our Arizona for a while and recuperate.

The Messrs Smith Brothers, who are opening a fine meat market north of Kelly & Stephens', received to-day from California, per express, a consignment of flounders, clams, crabs, etc., which were gobbled up with avidity by our citizens. The flounders sold at $1.25 per pound.

Humbug.—We will bet any one of our esteemed contemporaries in Arizona $5 to $1 that there is no such firm in existence as the Victor Well Auger and Rock Boring Manufacturing Company at 511 Walnut St., St. Louis, Missouri. The whole thing is a swindle.

The funeral of the pioneer, D. R. Poland, on Sunday, notwithstanding the bad weather, was largely attended. The remains were in charge of the Masons, and the last sad rites over the good citizen were performed at the burying ground of the Order. More than one moist eye we discovered as the body was consigned to earth and its last resting place. The will of the Lord is done, and a gentle, good man slumbers forever. A BARBOOM BUFFIAN.
The Sort of Amusement that Is Taken in a Frontier Saloon.
The Sort of Amusement that Is Taken in a Frontier Saloon.

The Alta Arizona contains the following account by Judge J. E. Stevens of a terrible shooting affair at Hackberry, A. T., on Feb. 20: Joseph Welden came into Hackberry about 10 A. M. He hired an Indian to hold his mule in an available place for a quick exit from town. His first recorded exploit was to try and get his work in on Edward Powers, who, thinking discretion the better part of valor, made good time out of range. His next demonstration was to order Bailey, the saloon-keeper, to hold up his hands, while Joe held his revolver at his head, cocked. This style of amusement lasted about an hour, when Dr. Day came into the saloon and invited Joe to drink. After the drinks, the Doctor attempted to put his hand in his pocket for money to pay, when Joe ordered him to hold up his hands, which the Doctor promptly did, at the same time sidling towards the door, through which he passed just as a bullet from Joe's pistol struck the casing on the left side of the door. Some half an hour later Day and John Bullock entered the saloon, when the Doctor said: "Joe, take a drink with us." Joe took his liquor in his left hand, holding his cocked pistol in his right, backed into the corner of the room and drank; returned and placed the glass on the counter, leaned against the counter with his pistol in his right hand laid across the counter, his left arm resting on it. In this position Joe ordered Bullock to approach him, which he did, when Joe said, "You have a pistol?" Bullock said "Yes," and with his left hand pulled a small five-shooter from his left coat pocket, changed it to his right hand and cocked it, holding it pointed towards Joe, who had his pistol against Bullock's breast. The next known occurrence was a discharge of Welden's pistol, followed by the retreat of Bullock, doubled up by the shot, and pursued by Joe with his pistol close to his back, into which he discharged two shots so close as to set fire to his clothing. Charley Spencer called on Joe to cease firing and surrender. Joe sent a shot so close to Charley as to graze his neck and ran toward his mule, when fire was opened upon him by citizens, and a shot struck him which brought him down.

South and West.
Montgomery, Ala., has just started up its first cotton factory. The event caused much enthusiasm.

The village of Prince Fredericktown, the county seat of Calvert county, Md., has been almost entirely destroyed by fire. Most of the county records were consumed.

Four men were blown to fragments by an explosion in the packing house of the Lake Superior Powder company at Marquette, Mich.

The Lumberman's exchange, at Chicago, Ill., reports that the past year has been one of the most successful ever experienced among lumbermen in the Northwest.

CAPTAIN EDWARD POSTAL, of the steamer Hard Cash, which arrived at Memphis, reports that the back water from the Mississippi river extended up the White river to Clarendon, Ark., a distance of 135 miles from the mouth, and the entire country intervening was under water, which was two feet higher than ever known before. Great loss of stock and damage to farming interests occurred throughout the White river bottoms. Reports come of great suffering in the overflowed districts.

In reply to the inquiry of the secretary of war as to the number of destitute people in his State, Judge Mangum, commissioner of Arkansas, estimates the number of persons in that State needing relief at 20,000. Commissioner Homingway, of Mississippi, named 18,000 as the number in that State. Add to these the 5,000 destitute in Tennessee, and it makes an aggregate of 43,000 persons whose condition is such as demands prompt attention at the hands of the government.

An anti-Chinese meeting, at which 30,000 persons were present, has been held in San Francisco. Resolutions petitioning Congress to restrict Chinese emigration were passed.

Forty thousand persons in the counties along the lower Mississippi have been left destitute by the recent floods.

The town of Nacori, Arizona, was attacked by Apache, and three persons were killed on each side.

John O. Massey and his wife, an old couple living near Charlottesville, Va., were killed and their money was taken from their house the other night.

The Illinois State board of agriculture reports that the seeding for the next wheat crop amounts to 2,676,000 acres, or 275,000 less than last year. The present condition, however, is most favorable.

Three alleged murderers were taken from the jail at Albuquerque, N. M., by masked men and hanged to trees.

The Iowa legislature has agreed to an amendment to strike out the word "male" from the constitution. If agreed to by the next legislature it will then go to the people.

Two Indians were hanged the other day at Lakeport, Cal., for murdering a white man.

The Michigan legislature has passed a bill appropriating $265,000 for the further relief of the sufferers by forest fires.

A Chicago dispatch says that Mr. Scoville declares that as soon as the bill of exceptions in Guiteau's case is ready he will retire from the defense. He says that there will be no difficulty in getting eminent counsel, but he does not know that General Butler will manage the case.

The Ohio river steamer Sidney, while making a trip from Cincinnati to Wheeling, W. Va., burst her main steam pipe. Mrs. Little and her grandson and a Mr. King were instantly killed, Mrs. Stephenson, wife of the boat's pilot, was fatally scalded, and five other persons were injured.

The number of deaths by the bursting of a steam pipe on the Ohio river steamer Sidney has increased to eight.

INFORMATION has been received at Raleigh, N. C., that the Mormons have made a lodgment near King's Mountain, that State. Numbers of the country people flocked to hear them and they made about fifty converts at that point.

LATER dispatches estimate that over 80,000 square miles of territory has been inundated by the floods in the Mississippi valley, and the total number of sufferers is placed at 60,000 persons. In Bolivar county, Miss., no less than thirty lives have been lost by drowning, and the whole county, containing about 11,000 persons, has been under water.
